extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in methodology and heuristic of proof (graduate students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying methodological criteria for how mathematical conjectures are tested, proved, criticised, and repaired — including the roles of counterexamples, definition-change, lemma-incorporation, and heuristic (informal) methods versus formalist approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as decomposition / quasi-experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'proof' may be a thought-experiment or 'quasi-experiment' which suggests a decomposition of the original conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas, embedding it in a possibly quite distant body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume such a proof establishes the absolute truth of the conjecture; instead treat it as analysis that generates lemmas to be tested. The proof may be heuristically useful even if some subconjectures are false. (Teacher: 'I do not think that it establishes the truth of the conjecture.'; 'proof...suggests a decomposition of the original conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas')

rubrics_metrics.name: Local versus global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish counterexamples that refute a lemma (local counterexamples) from those that refute the main conjecture itself (global counterexamples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A local-but-not-global counterexample criticises the proof (a lemma) without falsifying the conjecture; it signals where the proof must be repaired or the lemma refined. Tests should target the decomposed lemmas as well as the main conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring (rejection of counterexample by redefining terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of dismissing counterexamples by declaring them 'monsters' and redefining the concept (e.g. of 'polyhedron') so the counterexample no longer counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ad hoc strategy that sacrifices respect for counterexamples; it removes counterexamples by linguistic or definitional contraction rather than addressing substantive issues. Treat such redefinitions with suspicion — they may block learning from refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender (rejection of the conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon the conjecture when a genuine global counterexample is found that cannot be repaired by reasonable adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender is an honest outcome: if the conjecture is falsified, one may accept its falsity and move on rather than forcing ad hoc rescues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring / piecemeal exclusions / strategic withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve the conjecture by barring exceptional cases (explicitly excluding troublesome instances) or by piecemeal modification to avoid refutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a narrowed conjecture that may survive refutation, but can be ad hoc; evaluate whether exclusions are principled (theory-driven) or merely tactical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the counterexample (its interpretation or relevant terms) so that it no longer counts as a refutation, instead of changing the conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from monster-barring in that the monster is reinterpreted/adjusted; still risks ad hoc reasoning and should be justified by substantive conceptual work if accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving conjecture by lemma-incorporation (proof-generated theorem vs naive conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lemmas discovered during proof attempts to refine and incorporate into a stronger, more robust conjecture — producing a 'proof-generated theorem' rather than the naive original guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method often yields more reliable theorems because it reflects the structure uncovered by proof attempts; prefer conjectures that arise from and survive the proof-construction process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of refutations in proof-elaboration and theorem-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutations (counterexamples) play a constructive role: they drive the elaboration of proofs and the formation of better theorems; there is an 'alliance of proof and refutations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories and proofs by how they respond to refutation: productive engagement with counterexamples (leading to conceptual change or stronger theorems) is a mark of healthy methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductive structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of reductive (reduction-to-simpler-cases) reasoning and structures in analysing proofs and conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reduction is legitimate for the class of objects considered (e.g. whether the reduction preserves the relevant invariants), and watch for hidden assumptions when reducing to simpler cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallibilism (mathematical fallibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit acceptance that mathematical conjectures and proofs are fallible; discovery proceeds by conjecture, criticism, and improvement rather than by infallible deduction alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological stance: prefer procedures that allow for revision, testing, and conceptual development rather than treating proofs as final and unchallengeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-formation and definitional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and mathematical concepts should be judged by their role in problem-solving and their responsiveness to counterexamples; definitions often evolve (contracted, expanded, or made implicit) during the debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counterexamples emerge, consider conceptual revision as a legitimate methodological tool, but distinguish principled conceptual development from ad hoc tinkering intended merely to save a conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility versus sophistication of conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausible or 'trivially true' conjectures are often quickly refuted; by contrast, sophisticated or implausible conjectures, matured through criticism, may better capture deep truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake initial plausibility for robustness; evaluate conjectures by their survival under systematic criticism and their explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive testing / corroboration prior to proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures should be tested in many cases (corroboration) before and during attempts at proof, as testing helps to reveal structure and potential counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing is heuristic evidence supporting conjectures but is not a substitute for proof; use testing to guide proof-strategy and lemma-formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic methods versus formalist metamathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology should account for informal, situational, heuristic modes of mathematical discovery (Pólya-style) rather than identifying mathematics entirely with its formal/metamathematical abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methods on whether they illuminate informal discovery, problem-solving heuristics, and concept-formation, not only formal derivability or decision-procedure mechanisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-experiment (quasi-experiment) as legitimate argumentative form
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought-experiments that transform objects (e.g. stretching a polyhedral surface) can serve as proofs or proof-ideas that decompose conjectures into testable lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such thought-experiments as heuristic proofs: useful for generating lemmas and strategies, but scrutinise the steps (e.g. whether operations preserve invariants) and identify hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for constructive instructions and existence of procedures (e.g. ordering for triangle removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof relies on an operation (e.g. 'remove triangles in an order preserving V-E+F'), the existence and constructive method for that ordering must be specified, not merely asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof gives a method to carry out the required steps; lack of constructive instruction is a vulnerability exploited by local counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful treatment of counterexamples (avoid purely verbal rescues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples should be treated with respect as potential sources of conceptual and theoretical improvement rather than being expelled by mere verbal or definitional tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer responses to refutation that produce theory growth (lemma incorporation, principled exceptions, conceptual clarification) over mere contraction of terms that hides the problem.
